title: Lost in the Mix: Evaluating LLM Understanding of Code-Switched Text
venue: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
problem_statement: How Large Language Models (LLMs) comprehend and reason over code-switched (mixed-language) text across different switching directions, language pairs, and linguistic constraints, and whether multilingual proficiency reflects genuine semantic comprehension or superficial pattern matching.
domain: Natural Language Processing, Large Language Models, Code-Switching and Code-Mixing, Multilingual Language Understanding, Reading Comprehension, Multi-Domain Reasoning, Natural Language Inference
theoretical_framework: Sociolinguistic and grammatical theories of code-switching, specifically the Equivalence Constraint Theory (Poplack, 1978) and the Matrix Language Frame model (Myers-Scotton, 1993), which govern permissible grammatical boundaries, matrix language frame preservation, and syntactic well-formedness in mixed-language discourse.
methodology: A controlled multi-step LLM-centric generation pipeline using Claude 3.5 Sonnet to construct linguistically grounded noun-token code-switched variants (governed by Equivalence Constraint Theory and Matrix Language Frame rules) and random ratio-token (20%) variants of Belebele, MMLU, and XNLI across five typologically diverse languages (English, Arabic, German, French, Chinese); systematic zero-shot benchmarking across eight open-source LLMs (LLaMA 3.2 3B, LLaMA 3.1 8B/70B, Qwen 2.5 3B/7B/72B, Mistral 7B v0.3, ALLaM 7B) using EleutherAI LM Evaluation Harness; switching-direction ablations reversing matrix and embedded languages; extreme multilingual mixing ablations blending two to four embedded languages; and mitigation studies comparing instructional in-context learning (ICL) prompts against instruction fine-tuning on 14.6k synthetic code-switched TED Talk samples using LLaMA 3.1 8B.
datasets: Belebele (parallel reading comprehension benchmark across English, Arabic, German, French, and Chinese)
MMLU / MMMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding multi-choice reasoning benchmark)
TED Talks Parallel Corpus (Qi et al., 2018; filtered English sentences >70 words with parallel Arabic, Chinese, French, and German translations used for instruction tuning)

metrics: Accuracy (proportion of correctly answered questions per benchmark)
Weighted Average Accuracy (size-weighted mean accuracy across Belebele, MMLU, and XNLI)
Accuracy Delta (performance difference between code-switched variant and monolingual baseline)
Human Preference and LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-4o) pairwise preference ratings for generation quality
baseline_comparisons: Monolingual English Baseline (accuracy: 0.54 to 0.70 across models)
Monolingual Non-English Baselines (Arabic, German, French, Chinese)
Placeholder Baseline ('####' token substitutions isolating structural disruption from foreign semantics; accuracy: 0.41 to 0.59)

key_results.noun_token_csw_en_matrix: Accuracy consistently drops across all models (LLaMA 3B: 0.47-0.50 vs 0.54; LLaMA 70B: 0.66-0.67 vs 0.70; Qwen 72B: 0.65-0.66 vs 0.69). All models outperform placeholder baselines.
key_results.ratio_token_csw_en_matrix: Random 20% token substitutions cause comparable degradation to noun substitutions (LLaMA 3B: 0.43-0.51 vs 0.54; LLaMA 70B: 0.67-0.68 vs 0.70; Qwen 72B: 0.66 vs 0.69).
key_results.reverse_csw_non_en_matrix: Embedding English tokens into non-English matrix sentences consistently improves accuracy for lower-resource conditions (Mistral 7B Arabic: 0.35 to 0.48; Qwen 3B Arabic: 0.40 to 0.48; ALLaM 7B Chinese: 0.44 to 0.51).
key_results.extreme_multilingual_mixing: Mixing 2 to 4 languages in English matrix sentences reduces MMLU accuracy by 0.03 to 0.07 across models regardless of script type.
key_results.icl_mitigation: Yields inconsistent results (+0.01 to +0.07 for Qwen and ALLaM; -0.01 to -0.18 for LLaMA and Mistral).
key_results.model_finetuning_mitigation: Fine-tuning LLaMA 8B on 14.6k CSW generation samples produces consistent accuracy gains on comprehension benchmarks across all embedded languages while preserving monolingual English accuracy.

key_findings: Linguistically constrained code-switching systematically impairs comprehension: inserting foreign noun tokens into English sentences consistently degrades LLM accuracy across all evaluated model families, scales, and reasoning tasks, even when switches strictly adhere to Equivalence Constraint Theory and Matrix Language Frame rules.

Asymmetry in code-switching direction reveals an English-centric representational bias: while embedding non-English tokens into English matrix sentences reduces performance, embedding English tokens into non-English matrix sentences consistently improves comprehension (for example, Mistral 7B accuracy increases from 0.35 to 0.48 in Arabic), indicating that English acts as a facilitative anchor in multilingual pretraining representations.

Syntactic well-formedness provides limited mitigation: random ratio-token substitutions (20%) cause degradation comparable in magnitude to linguistically grounded noun-token substitutions, demonstrating that performance decline stems from representational interference in multilingual token integration rather than purely grammatical disruption.

Meaningful foreign tokens outperform semantic disruption: all models score substantially higher on code-switched inputs than on placeholder baselines ('####'), proving that LLMs partially recover and leverage semantic information from embedded foreign tokens.

In-context learning (ICL) mitigation yields inconsistent, architecture-dependent effects: meta-instruction cues improve performance for models with extensive multilingual pretraining (Qwen and ALLaM, gaining up to +0.07), but degrade performance for models with less cross-lingual alignment (LLaMA and Mistral, dropping up to -0.18).

Model-based instruction fine-tuning on synthetic CSW data provides robust, stable recovery: fine-tuning LLaMA 8B on 14.6k synthetic code-switched generation samples yields consistent accuracy gains across all embedded languages on downstream comprehension tasks without sacrificing monolingual English accuracy.
scope_and_delimitations: The study focuses on evaluating LLM comprehension and reasoning on multi-choice question answering and natural language inference rather than generative conversational dialogue or surface-level classification tasks.

Evaluations are delimited to five typologically diverse languages (English as primary matrix, alongside Arabic, German, French, and Chinese) representing varying scripts, families, and pretraining data representation levels.

Code-switching generation is primarily delimited to intra-sentential noun-token substitutions adhering to Equivalence Constraint Theory (ECT) and Matrix Language Frame (MLF) models, alongside a 20% random ratio-token substitution setup.
Evaluations are restricted to eight open-weight instruction-tuned decoder-only LLMs (LLaMA 3.2 3B, LLaMA 3.1 8B/70B, Qwen 2.5 3B/7B/72B, Mistral 7B v0.3, ALLaM 7B).

Evaluation datasets rely on synthetic code-switched variants generated from parallel multilingual benchmark corpora (Belebele, MMLU, XNLI) rather than naturalistic spontaneous human conversational transcripts.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: While our study adopts a controlled evaluation setup for both linguistically and non-linguistically motivated code-switching, the noun-token approach we employ reflects one of the fundamental forms of linguistically grounded, naturalistic switching. However, more complex forms of codeswitching may induce more severe performance degradation. Future work should investigate how higher-complexity switching patterns affect LLMs' understanding. Additionally, in our non-linguistically motivated ratio-token experiments, the substitution rate was fixed at 20%. Exploring how variation in this ratio affects model behavior could yield a more nuanced understanding of the impact of non-linguistically grounded switching on LLM comprehension. Finally, our benchmarks are synthetically constructed yet human-verified to ensure linguistic naturalness, and this controlled design enables reproducible analysis of how LLMs process mixedlanguage inputs, even if it does not capture all nuances of spontaneous human code-switching.
limitations.summary: The authors acknowledge that their evaluation relies on noun-token substitutions, which represents only a basic form of linguistically grounded switching, whereas more complex switching structures could cause greater degradation; the random ratio-token experiment is restricted to a single fixed substitution rate of 20% without testing rate variations; and the benchmarks are synthetically generated from parallel corpora, which, despite human verification, may not capture all nuances, informalities, and pragmatic dynamics of spontaneous human code-switching.

generalizability_gap: The findings are restricted to five high-to-mid resource languages (English, Arabic, German, French, and Chinese) and do not evaluate low-resource language pairs, dialects (such as regional Arabic or colloquial Tagalog-English/Hinglish), or trilingual and multi-party conversational settings. Additionally, the study evaluates only synthetic intra-sentential noun substitutions and 20% random token replacements, leaving open how models generalize to spontaneous conversational code-switching, clause-level switching, speech/multimodal inputs, or low-resource non-Latin scripts.
methodological_gap: The study relies on synthetic LLM-generated code-switched benchmarks constructed from parallel corpora rather than authentic human-generated code-switched dialogues; it tests a fixed 20% substitution rate for random switching rather than exploring a continuous spectrum of switch densities; and it investigates fine-tuning mitigation on a single architecture and scale (LLaMA 3.1 8B) on a relatively small corpus (14.6k samples) without evaluating pretraining-stage code-switched objectives or larger multi-model fine-tuning suites.
future_work: Investigating how higher-complexity switching patterns (such as phrase-level, clause-level, and inter-sentential code-switching) affect LLM comprehension.
Exploring variations in token substitution rates across a wider spectrum to systematically measure the dose-response relationship between switch density and model degradation.

Developing and evaluating pretraining paradigms and scalable instruction-tuning regimes that natively incorporate code-switching as a first-class linguistic phenomenon to mitigate English-centric representational bias.
Extending code-switching evaluation frameworks to spontaneous conversational human datasets, low-resource language pairs, and spoken or multimodal interaction settings.
